Neonates of the short-finned pilot whale (Globicephala macrorhynchus) are among the largest odontocete calves at birth, with a recorded length of 139.5 centimeters [Lb = 139.5 centimeters], a dimension that reflects an extended gestation within the warm-bodied physiology of the mother. Newborn calves exhibit a wet weight of 37,000 grams [Wwb = 37,000 grams], a substantial mass that provides them with sufficient lipid reserves for the energetically demanding period of early nursing. Field data indicate that the gestation period lasts 730 days [tg = 730 days] at the species' core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], a duration that aligns with the prolonged fetal development observed in other large, deep-diving delphinids. This extended in utero phase is thought to facilitate the development of a thick blubber layer and the advanced neuromuscular coordination needed for immediate swimming and synchronous respiration with the mother following parturition. The combination of a large neonate and a lengthy gestation period is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity, a pattern common among pelagic, long-lived cetaceans with low annual reproductive output.

Female short-finned pilot whales attain sexual maturity after a prolonged juvenile period, with the onset of puberty recorded at approximately 3,285 days since birth [tp = approximately 3,285 days since birth] under the stable thermal conditions of their internal environment at 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. At this developmental milestone, females typically measure 315.6 centimeters [Lp = 315.6 centimeters] in length and have a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 391,000 grams [Wwp = 391,000 grams]. Males follow a distinctly slower maturation trajectory, reaching puberty at about 5,292.5 days since birth [tp = about 5,292.5 days since birth] at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], by which point they have grown to 401 centimeters [Lp = 401 centimeters] and weigh approximately 781,000 grams [Wwp = approximately 781,000 grams]. This marked sexual dimorphism in both the timing of maturation and the size at which it occurs suggests that males require additional years of growth to attain the body size necessary for successful competition in a polygynous mating system. The pronounced delay in male puberty relative to females is a recurring theme in the life history of sexually dimorphic cetaceans, often linked to intrasexual selection pressure.

The ultimate length attained by adult females in this species reaches 364.7 centimeters [Li = 364.7 centimeters], a size that is accompanied by a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 593,000 grams [Wwi = 593,000 grams]. Adult males, however, grow considerably larger, reaching a maximum recorded length of 480 centimeters [Li = 480 centimeters] and an ultimate wet weight of 1,260,000 grams [Wwi = 1,260,000 grams], reflecting a pronounced degree of sexual dimorphism that is among the most extreme within the genus Globicephala. This size disparity is thought to be driven by male-male competition for access to receptive females, as larger males are more likely to dominate reproductive aggregations. The steep growth trajectory leading to these asymptotic dimensions is sustained by a diet dominated by squid and deep-water fish, which provides the high caloric density necessary for maintaining such a bulky physiques in an energetic environment characterized by deep, frequent foraging dives. The ultimate wet weight in males, exceeding 1.2 metric tons, underscores the substantial metabolic demands placed on these animals throughout their extended lifespan.

Reproductive output in short-finned pilot whales is exceptionally low among mammals, with females producing a single calf per litter [N_R_i = single calf per litter] and typically yielding only one litter every five years [F_R_i = one litter every five years] under the thermal conditions of their core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This maximum rate of reproduction, equivalent to a single offspring every half-decade, positions this species at the extreme slow end of the life-history continuum, comparable to other large, long-lived cetaceans such as sperm whales and killer whales. The extended inter-birth interval is likely a consequence of both the high energetic investment required for a 730-day gestation (730 days) [tg = 730 days] and the prolonged period of maternal care that follows parturition at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. Calves begin the transition to nutritional independence after a weaning period that occurs 730 days since birth [tx = 730 days since birth] at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], but they often remain in close association with their mother for several additional years, learning complex foraging techniques and social behaviors critical for survival in a fission-fusion society.

Maximum longevity for short-finned pilot whales is considerable, with the oldest documented individuals persisting for approximately 22,995 days [am = approximately 22,995 days] when maintained at a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], a lifespan equivalent to roughly 63 years. This extreme longevity is consistent with the species' slow pace of life, which integrates a protracted maturation period, the lowest reproductive rate among delphinids, and a high degree of social cohesion. Post-reproductive females are commonly observed in pilot whale pods, a phenomenon that has attracted considerable interest from evolutionary biologists studying the adaptive value of extended lifespan beyond reproductive cessation. The species' large brain size and complex social structure have been linked to this long life span, as selection may favor individuals capable of accumulating ecological knowledge over decades and transmitting it to younger kin. Field studies using photo-identification and genetic sampling have confirmed that both male and female pilot whales can survive several decades after reaching sexual maturity, contributing to the multigenerational structure that characterizes their stable social units.
